name: PT. Gajah Tunggal Tbk

frontmatter.title: Gajah Tunggal: a tyre franchise priced for the end of its earnings
frontmatter.summary: Gajah Tunggal is Southeast Asia's largest tyre maker, sells GT Radial in more than 90.0 countries and has served Indonesia's replacement market for decades. We cut the FY2026E gross margin to 18.1% after a weak third quarter; nine-month sales still grew 9.1% and profit 22.2%. At Rp1,115 the shares pay 3.3x earnings and 0.3x book, our bear-case value. We maintain BUY with a Rp2,463 target.
thesis: The vendor data understates earnings: its depreciation line is a fraction of the audited charge and its finance cost is understated. Restated, FY2025A EBITDA is 2,596 IDR bn and operating cash flow of 2,018 IDR bn covered net profit of 1,243.2, so the margin slide is a forecasting question, not an accounting one - though the nine-month working-capital build, now funded largely by a near-doubling of supplier credit, is the balance-sheet fact that tests it [S3, S6, S7].

Demand is real: nine-month 2026 net sales rose 9.1% and net profit 22.2% on the domestic replacement channel, GAIKINDO wholesales reached 679,020 units in the first nine months against 803,687 units in FY2025A, and the association targets 850,000 units for the year [S8].
The balance sheet is not distressed: net debt is 2.0x EBITDA, equity is 11,167 IDR bn, there is no minority interest and the FY2025A dividend of Rp80.0 a share was paid in cash [S7, S0].

The price embeds a control discount more than an operating one: related-party sales were 16.0% of net sales in FY2025A and rose again in the nine months, Denham holds 49.5% and Michelin 10.0% - a majority strategic block - with public shareholders outside it at 34.5% and Drs Lo Kheng Hong at 5.9% [S3, S4].

The target is still cheap against the balance sheet: Rp2,463 is a fraction of the 3,260.9 of equity per share, and the price is a small fraction of it, so the call is a re-rating to a discount rather than to a premium, and the twelve-month carry is not what produces it [S0].

catalysts.event: Full-year 2026 results and annual report, disclosing the year-end related-party revenue ratio and the TBR utilisation
First-quarter 2027 volumes, the first read on whether the domestic replacement cycle holds after the rebound
Annual shareholders meeting and the FY2026 dividend decision
Unaudited first-half 2027 financials, showing whether the annual price adjustment has restored the gross margin

blocks.text: We maintain our BUY on PT Gajah Tunggal Tbk with a twelve-month target of Rp2,463, which is 127.6% above the Rp1,115 at which the shares last traded [S0]. The company is the largest tyre maker in Southeast Asia by its own description, with installed capacity of 55.0 k tyres/day passenger car radials and 3.2 k tyres/day truck and bus radials, plus bias and motorcycle lines, and it sells under its own GT Radial brand in more than 90.0 countries [S3]. The franchise is the domestic replacement market, where motorcycle tyres have met most of Indonesian demand since production began and where the buyer replaces a worn part rather than negotiating an annual price [S3]. Export sales are the smaller channel and the one most exposed to trade policy [S3, S4].

This results update adds the September 2026 quarter and lowers the FY2026E gross margin to 18.1% from the level the initiation carried. The filing behind the quarter is the same three-page 30 September 2026 statement the initiation used, so revenue of 14,323 IDR bn, gross profit of 2,641 IDR bn on an 18.4% margin and net profit of 965 IDR bn are the figures already in the forecast [S7, S6]. The quarter itself is the informative part: the stand-alone gross margin fell again as raw-material costs rose from the second quarter and the annual price adjustment lagged, and the third quarter's profit fell sharply against the second quarter even as revenue reached the highest level in the file [S0, S6]. We now carry a fourth quarter above that trough but below the nine-month average, and well below the margin the prior-year fourth quarter earned, rather than the seasonal rebound the earlier draft assumed: that draft's full-year margin required a one-quarter recovery larger than any sequential move in the pack, in a quarter in which [S9] reports input costs still rising [S0, S7, S9]. Full-year profit of 1,183.4 therefore sits below the vendor's last-twelve-month figure, which contains the strongest quarter of 2025 [S0, S3]. The target moves with both the lower margin and the refreshed market block [S0].

The disagreement with the price is about whether the earnings can be sustained, not about the next quarter. At Rp1,115 the shares trade at 3.3x our FY2026E earnings, 3.5x EBITDA, 0.3x book and a 6.7% forward dividend yield, on a market capitalisation of IDR3,885.2bn [S0]. Those multiples say the market expects the earnings to stop: net debt is 2.0x EBITDA, but net borrowing of Rp900.0bn in FY2026E funds the capacity expansion before turning to repayment from FY2029E as capex falls below operating cash flow [S3, S7].

Three things move the value from here. The first is raw-material pass-through: natural rubber, synthetic rubber, tyre cord and carbon black were 29.9%, 21.4%, 10.8% and 16.8% of the tyre division's raw-material cost in FY2025A, and the company describes an annual price adjustment that considers competitors' positions rather than a formula [S3, S9]. Nine-month 2026 gross margin was 18.4%, below the audited FY2025A 20.1%, which is the lag in action [S7]. The second is the domestic cycle: 679,020 units wholesales in the first nine months against 803,687 units in FY2025A, with the association targeting 850,000 units for the year, is the cleanest read on new-vehicle demand [S8]. The third is governance, which is where the discount lives: local sales to related parties multiplied nearly tenfold in the nine months while third-party local sales fell, and related-party trade receivables stood at 3,951 IDR bn against third-party receivables of 1,578 IDR bn [S4, S7].

We are not dismissing the governance issue. It is the reason a company with 11,167 IDR bn of equity and 2,596 IDR bn of EBITDA trades below book, and it is why our target is only a low-single-digit multiple of earnings rather than a peer multiple. The point is that the discount is applied in the price, and our base case does not assume the margin stays at the nine-month trough: it recovers from 18.4% to the FY2025A 20.1% only by FY2029E, a year later than the last audited margin, and we hold a related-party receivable allowance in the bridge sized on the three GITI trading companies' balances rather than on a blended book [S0, S3, S7, S9].

A tyre is a consumable disguised as a component. A motorist replaces a set every few years, a truck fleet rotates them by season, and on Indonesian roads a motorcycle tyre wears quickly. That gives a maker with a broad catalogue and deep distributor reach a replacement annuity, because the vehicle assembler specifies the size and the workshop chooses on availability and brand trust rather than on the invoice price alone. The replacement market is also insulated from the new-vehicle cycle: a weak year for car sales does not stop a large vehicle park from needing fresh rubber, which is why a tyre maker can grow while the factory-fitted channel shrinks. The counterweight is capital intensity. A tyre plant lasts decades, depreciation is a large slice of cost, and adding capacity takes years, so the industry alternates between tight periods that pay for the plant and loose periods that do not.

PT Gajah Tunggal Tbk was founded in 1951, is headquartered in Jakarta and manufactures in West Java, and describes itself as the largest tyre maker in Southeast Asia [S3]. It produces passenger car radials for cars, SUVs and pick-ups, truck and bus radials for commercial vehicles, bias tyres, and motorcycle tyres under the IRC licence and its own Zeneos brand, as well as non-tyre products including tyre cord, synthetic rubber and nylon filament yarn [S3]. In FY2025A passenger car radials were the largest line at 5,568 IDR bn of sales, motorcycle tyres contributed 5,364 IDR bn, bias tyres 3,779 IDR bn, truck and bus radials 2,252 IDR bn and non-tyre products 352 IDR bn [S3].

The brands carry the franchise. GT Radial is the passenger and SUV brand, distributed across Indonesia through more than 40.0 distributors and exported to more than 90.0 countries, and it is fitted as original equipment by several assemblers in Indonesia [S3]. IRC is the licensed motorcycle brand and Zeneos the company's own, and between them they hold a large share of the domestic replacement market for motorcycle tyres, a segment where production began in 1971 and where the company says it meets most domestic demand [S3]. The TireZone retail chain is the company's own outlet channel [S3].

Vertical integration is the structural feature. The company produces synthetic rubber and tyre cord itself, with capacity of 75,000 tonnes of synthetic rubber a year plus its own tyre cord and nylon lines, and it consumed most of that output internally in FY2025A, which reduces dependence on external suppliers and captures part of the conversion margin [S3]. Total tyre production was 40.3 m tyres in FY2025A, of which 9.7 m tyres passenger car radials, 27.0 m tyres motorcycle tyres and the balance bias and truck radials [S3]. Sales volumes were 9.9 m tyres passenger car radials, 26.9 m tyres motorcycle tyres, 2.8 m tyres bias tyres and 0.7 m tyres truck and bus radials, a mix that makes the company a motorcycle-tyre business by unit volume and a passenger-car business by value [S3].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Denham Pte Ltd, whose majority shareholder is GITI Tire Pte Ltd, holds 49.5% of the shares, Compagnie Financiere Michelin holds 10.0%, and public shareholders outside the block hold 34.5%, with Drs Lo Kheng Hong at 5.9% [S3]. Denham and Michelin together are a majority strategic block; the public float is the balance, not the free-float figure the vendor data shows [S3]. The group employs 17,626 people, operates its own polytechnic to train staff, and consolidates two subsidiaries, PT Filamendo Sakti and PT Prima Sentra Megah, alongside associates including PT Polychem Indonesia and a small stake in PT Speedwork Solusi Utama, a trading and e-commerce company that is also a customer [S3, S5]. The FY2025A accounts were audited by KAP Liana Ramon Xenia & Rekan with an unmodified opinion [S3].

The strategy is capacity-led. The company lifted truck and bus radial capacity in FY2025A to 3.2 k tyres/day, funded a capex programme of Rp2,271.0bn, and has announced a plan for a second plant in Karawang to make tyres for electric vehicles, with an indicative investment the president director put at about ten trillion rupiah [S3, S5]. Passenger car radial utilisation was about three-fifths of available capacity in FY2025A and motorcycle utilisation was close to full, so volume growth in the largest segment can be met from existing plant before new capacity is needed [S3].

The Indonesian tyre market is large, domestic and replacement-led. The passenger car and truck tyre market was 30.2 m tyres in FY2025A, against vehicle wholesales of 803,687 units cars and 6,412,769 units motorcycles in the same year, which means the replacement pool is many times the new-vehicle flow [S3]. The tyre market grew modestly in FY2025A, with replacement demand growing faster than the factory-fitted channel, and the board describes the domestic outlook as positive while warning that it will intensify competition [S3].

New-vehicle demand has recovered strongly. GAIKINDO wholesales were 679,020 units in the first nine months of 2026, up by a fifth on the prior year, and the association targets 850,000 units for the full year against 803,687 units sold in FY2025A [S8]. The recovery matters for two channels: the original-equipment fitments that tyre makers win at the assembler, and the replacement demand that follows a growing vehicle park with a lag. Motorcycle sales of 6,412,769 units in FY2025A are the larger unit market and the one where Gajah Tunggal's share is strongest [S3]. The house macro desk nevertheless tilts away from Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer discretionary, and that tilt deserves an answer here: Gajah Tunggal's sales are replacement-led, so higher rates reach it through the consumer's wallet and the distributor's credit before they reach its own interest line - which is why we carry the demand risk in the bear case rather than cut the base for it.

Cost is the competitive battlefield. Raw materials were 68.0% of total production cost in FY2025A, with labour, energy and depreciation the next largest items and depreciation at 4.7% of production cost; within raw materials, natural rubber was 29.9%, synthetic rubber 21.4%, carbon black 16.8% and tyre cord 10.8% [S3]. Natural rubber is a plantation commodity priced in US dollars, carbon black and synthetic rubber track oil and butadiene, and the rupiah adds a second layer of exposure, which is why a tyre maker's margin moves with commodities it does not control and why the annual price adjustment matters more than volume [S3, S9].

The competitive set is a mix of global majors and regional specialists, and the company's own claim to advantage is location and integration rather than brand premium: its plants sit close to the natural rubber it buys, and its synthetic rubber and tyre cord lines give it cost control that an assembler-only competitor does not have [S3]. The moat is therefore a cost and distribution moat rather than a technology moat, and it is strongest in the domestic replacement market where the distributor network and the brand are hard to replicate [S3]. The threat is imported tyres, particularly from lower-cost producers, and the export channel is where trade policy bites [S3].

The tyre industry runs on a simple economics: the replacement market is roughly three to four times the size of the original-equipment market by volume, because every car built is eventually re-shod several times, while the factory-fitted channel is a single sale per vehicle. That is why tyre makers fight for shelf space at distributors and why a brand that a workshop trusts is worth more than a discount. It is also why the industry is cyclical in a peculiar way: demand is steady but capacity is lumpy, so a wave of investment across the industry compresses prices for several years and then a demand upturn fills the plants again. Indonesia adds two twists, a very large motorcycle population and a domestic natural-rubber supply, which together make it one of the few countries where a local maker can compete on cost with the global majors.

Revenue fell from Rp18,029.2bn in FY2024A to Rp17,664.2bn in FY2025A, a decline the board attributes to weaker export demand, while net profit rose from Rp1,186.9bn to Rp1,243.2bn on lower finance costs of 454 IDR bn against 685 IDR bn a year earlier and a foreign-exchange gain [S3]. The gross margin compressed from 21.5% to 20.1% as raw-material costs rose and the rupiah weakened, and that compression is the central fact of the forecast [S3]. Capex of Rp2,271.0bn exceeded depreciation of Rp802.8bn by a wide margin, which is the signature of a company investing through the cycle [S3].

The restatement of the data pack matters more here than in most names. The vendor's depreciation for FY2025A is a small fraction of the audited charge of Rp802.8bn, which spans manufacturing, selling and administrative allocations, and its finance cost is below the 454 IDR bn in the income statement [S3]. We register the audited figures as facts and the engine rebuilds EBITDA, which is why our FY2025A EBITDA of Rp2,649.0bn sits close to the 2,596 IDR bn the company reports, rather than the much lower figure the raw pack implies [S3]. Depreciation is set at 4.5% of revenue in FY2026E and eases to 4.4% by FY2030E as the asset base grows.

The nine months of 2026 are the anchor for the forecast. Revenue was 14,323 IDR bn, gross profit 2,641 IDR bn on an 18.4% margin, EBITDA 1,962 IDR bn and net profit 965 IDR bn, with finance costs down to 300 IDR bn and selling expenses of 761 IDR bn [S7]. The pack's quarterly rows are the only quarter-level evidence and they sum exactly to the filed nine months: the stand-alone margin was at its best in the first quarter, fell in the second as raw-material costs rose, and fell again to the lowest level in the file in the third, taking the nine-month margin to 18.4%, below the prior-year nine months [S0, S6]. We carry the fourth quarter at a slower growth rate than the third quarter's because the prior-year fourth quarter already contained a strong domestic push, giving FY2026E revenue of Rp19,077.3bn, or 8.0% growth, and a gross margin of 18.1%: that requires the fourth quarter above the third-quarter trough but below the nine-month average, which is the seasonal recovery this company has delivered before, without assuming a repeat of the exceptional prior-year fourth quarter [S0, S6]. From FY2027E growth slows to 4.0% because the nine-month surge is a shift inside local sales - related-party local sales rose to 3,140 IDR bn while third-party local sales fell to 8,620 IDR bn - not a widening of the market, and the Indonesian tyre market grew only modestly in FY2025A with replacement demand ahead of the factory-fitted channel [S3, S4]. The margin recovers to 20.1% only by FY2029E, the last audited level, because [S9] reports raw-material prices still rising at a double-digit rate in July 2026 and the company absorbing them; no part of the terminal value depends on a margin above history [S3, S4, S9].

The nine-month actuals against the full-year forecast are the first checkpoint. Revenue of 14,323 IDR bn is about three-quarters of the 19,077.3 we forecast for FY2026E; gross profit of 2,641 IDR bn is about three-quarters of the full-year 3,453.0; company-reported EBITDA of 1,962 IDR bn is about four-fifths of our restated 2,510.6; and net profit of 965 IDR bn is about four-fifths of 1,183.4 [S7, S6, S0]. The ratios differ in a consistent way: each profit line carries a slightly higher share of the year than revenue, because the fourth quarter is carried below the nine-month margin. So the year needs no rebound above the nine-month margin - it needs the fourth quarter to beat the third-quarter trough, and the third quarter shows how much of even that depends on the annual price adjustment landing [S0, S9].

Operating leverage is the reason profit grows faster than sales. Selling and administrative costs were 761 IDR bn plus the administration line in the nine months, about 9.5% of revenue, and the ratio is held flat thereafter because no cost programme is disclosed [S7, S3]. Working capital is the offset, and it is now funded by suppliers. Inventories were 3,461 IDR bn at the end of September against 2,576 IDR bn at the year-end, related-party trade receivables 3,951 IDR bn against 2,947 IDR bn, third-party receivables 1,578 IDR bn against 1,771 IDR bn, and trade payables rose to 3,860 IDR bn from 2,049 IDR bn [S7]. That is new supplier credit of more than four-fifths of the opening payable balance against a cost of sales increase of about a tenth, so the gross build in inventories and related-party receivables is almost entirely offset by payables. That is why the net working-capital ratio moves less than the gross lines, and we hold it at 20.1% of revenue [S7]. The filing is a three-page statement with no cash-flow statement, so nine-month operating cash flow cannot be computed from it and the cash conversion we can measure is the balance-sheet one - which rests on the suppliers continuing to fund the build. Payables normalising toward the FY2025A days is an explicit shock in the bear case [S7].

The balance sheet carries the expansion. Cash was 828 IDR bn at the end of September, equity 11,167 IDR bn, investments in associates 517 IDR bn, and debt rose over the nine months as the capex year and the dividend were funded with bank facilities after the US dollar notes were refinanced into rupiah in January 2025 [S7, S3]. Net debt is 2.0x EBITDA in FY2026E, which is comfortable for a company with this asset base, and the interest cover is strong because the finance cost has fallen year on year [S7].

Earnings quality is mixed and we flag it. In the audited year the earnings were cash-backed: operating cash flow of 2,018 IDR bn in FY2025A covered net profit of 1,243.2, and 1,835 IDR bn in FY2024A covered 1,186.9; the audit opinion is unmodified [S3]. The nine months of 2026 changed the balance-sheet mix rather than the cash cover. Inventories of 3,461 IDR bn are a third higher than at the year-end and related-party trade receivables of 3,951 IDR bn are more than double third-party receivables of 1,578 IDR bn, but the gross build is offset by payables of 3,860 IDR bn against 2,049 IDR bn, so the net working-capital build is smaller than the period's net profit of 965 IDR bn [S7]. That means the build is borrowed from suppliers, not that the profit is unbacked - and it also means the suppliers hold the switch. The related-party book is the part we do not take at face: it turns roughly five times slower than the third-party book, 2,101 IDR bn of it is owed by GITI Tire (USA) alone, and a one-quarter allowance on the balance would absorb about four-fifths of FY2026E net profit; we carry a probability-weighted allowance of that kind in the valuation bridge [S7, S3]. Related-party sales were 16.0% of net sales in FY2025A, and in the nine months of 2026 local related-party sales rose to 3,140 IDR bn while third-party local sales fell to 8,620 IDR bn, which is a structural shift rather than a seasonal one [S4, S3].

The industry registry sets the method card VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY for auto components, with DCF on free cash flow to the firm as the primary method and P/E and EV/EBITDA as cross-checks; the weights are half, three tenths and one fifth in the registry, and we cut the P/E leg to a tenth because it is struck on the audited FY2025A profit rather than on the stronger last-twelve-month earnings (see below) [S3, S0]. That set fits a capital-intensive manufacturer with a discrete investment cycle: the DCF captures the capex step-down and the terminal economics, the two multiples check that the DCF is not an artefact of the discount rate, and neither dominates the answer.

The cost of capital is the largest single assumption, and the build has to be shown in full because one step in it is easy to miss. The starting point is the ten-year Indonesian government yield of 7.45%, from which the house method deducts the sovereign default spread of 1.62%: a government bond yield is not a risk-free rate where the sovereign can default, and leaving the spread in would charge the same country risk twice, once in the base rate and again in the country premium. The base rate is therefore 7.45% less 1.62%; adding 1.96 times the sum of the mature-market equity premium of 4.23% and the Indonesian country premium of 2.46% gives the cost of equity of 18.9%. The levered beta is the industry unlevered beta of 0.90 geared for a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.51, and with debt at 60.1% of the capital structure at a pre-tax cost of 9.4% the weighted average cost of capital is 12.0%; these inputs come from the house macro deck (as of 31 October 2026) and the industry registry, not from the vendor data [S3, S7]. That is above what the company actually pays: finance costs of 454 IDR bn in FY2025A and 300 IDR bn in the nine months of 2026 annualise to a high-single-digit effective rate on average debt, below the 9.4% the engine uses, because the US-dollar notes were refinanced into rupiah facilities in January 2025 [S3, S7]. The gap is a deliberate normalisation - the P&L rate is measured on average debt and benefits from the refinancing, while the discount rate must hold for the forecast period - and it is conservative: at the company's effective rate the WACC falls by about a percentage point and the DCF rises by roughly a quarter, which the sensitivity table shows at the bottom of its WACC band. The 60.1% debt weight is also an artefact of computing D/E on a market capitalisation we believe is depressed; at the model's own average forecast leverage the WACC is slightly lower and the DCF a few per cent higher, so the mispricing in the denominator is not what produces the value gap. The same market leverage shows up in the cost of equity of 18.9%, which sits above the house IDR band, and the engine uses that rate to carry the twelve-month target forward. We disclose it rather than adjust it, because both rates come from one capital structure: forcing the cost of equity to the top of the band would push the WACC - the rate that discounts every cash flow here - below the band's floor and add materially to the DCF, trading a conservative carry for an aggressive discount rate. At the model's own average forecast leverage the same inputs give a cost of equity just above the top of the band with the WACC inside it. Rolling the Rp2,046 base one year at the 12.0% cost of capital inside the house band and subtracting the Rp75 dividend gives a twelve-month target about six per cent below the Rp2,358 base target - the excess of the 18.9% we use over the band rate applied to that base - and a total return about twenty-two points below the 127.6% we publish, both still far above the cost of equity, so nothing in the BUY depends on the out-of-band carry. The carry is a small part of the gap to the price, and we do not use the cost of equity to justify the terminal growth; that is argued on the WACC, as the terminal-growth basis states [S3, S7].

The primary DCF value is Rp1,681 per share. Free cash flow to the firm is negative in FY2026E at Rp-707.7bn because capex of Rp2,403.7bn and the working-capital build exceed operating cash flow, turns positive in FY2027E at Rp165.5bn, and grows to more than a trillion rupiah a year by the end of the explicit period [S0]. The terminal value, struck at 3.5% growth, is 55.5% of the present value, which is normal for a company with a long-lived asset base and is not a sign that the value is a terminal-value artefact: the explicit period already produces more than two-fifths of the value [S0]. The DCF value is convex in the gross margin, and sharply so: capex is a fixed share of revenue, so at a sustained trough margin the free cash flow after capex cannot service the debt and the equity value falls to nothing, while a modest recovery is worth several times a modest decline. That convexity, not the discount rate, is why the scenario range is wide, and it is why we treat the DCF as a distribution rather than a point estimate [S0, S7]. The terminal growth is below the house default because the terminal ROE is about nine per cent against a WACC inside the house band; growth beyond 3.5% on those returns would not be value-accretive, and the sensitivity table shows the DCF at the lower end of the terminal-growth band, where it remains above the market price but no longer carries the terminal assumption [S3, S7].

The cross-checks sit above the DCF, and the divergence is informative. The P/E method applies 6.5x, the average of the peer median and the company's own trailing-history average (three annual observations for P/E, four for EV/EBITDA, not a five-year window), to FY2025A earnings of Rp1,243.2bn and produces Rp2,329, which is 38.6% above the DCF [S0]. That leg is conservative by construction: the registry strikes the cross-check on the last audited fiscal year, and the audited FY2025A profit is below the last-twelve-month figure the refreshed pack now builds, which includes the strongest quarter of 2025; on that higher base the same multiple would value the leg roughly a seventh higher, so we cut its weight to a tenth and treat it as a disclosed cross-check rather than a value driver [S0, S7, S3]. The EV/EBITDA method applies 5.0x to the restated FY2025A EBITDA of Rp2,649.0bn - not the vendor's EBITDA, which carries the depreciation error - and produces Rp2,539, which is 51.1% versus the DCF [S3]. It is the strongest of the two multiples because it uses the corrected earnings base, but it still depends on a multiple struck on a peer set that includes loss-makers and on the 60.1% debt weight in the bridge, which is why the DCF carries the majority weight. The leg deliberately pairs last fiscal year's EBITDA with the latest balance sheet's net debt: charging the debt added since FY2025A against a year-earlier earnings base understates the leg, and on FY2025A net debt it would be higher. The P/E leg takes no equivalent penalty because it does not touch net debt. We keep that pairing so both multiple legs lean the same way, and we do not claim the leg's full value in the blend [S0, S7].

The sensitivity grid is binding at the top of the WACC band, where the DCF value falls towards the market price. Even there the value exceeds it, which means the thesis does not rest on the exact discount rate. At lower WACC values the upside grows, and at the bottom of the band the DCF holds the full upside. The terminal-growth band likewise shows the DCF at the low end of the range, where it remains above the market price but no longer relies on the house default. On FX, the house macro deck has USD/IDR at Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E against Rp18,012/USD spot, but we do not model an FX gain: about a fifth of revenue is exported (1,770 IDR bn and 1,040 IDR bn of export sales against 14,323 IDR bn of nine-month net sales) while raw materials are 68.0% of production cost and are US-dollar priced, so a weaker rupiah raises both export revenue and input costs and the net effect is a margin question, not a clean tailwind; the annual report states that rupiah weakness raised production costs in FY2025A [S3, S4]. What the price implies is harder to defend than what we forecast, but the test that matters is the margin, not growth. The engine's reverse DCF flexes revenue growth only and cannot bracket the market price: even at the low end of its range the discounted value stays above the price, and we read that as evidence that the gap is not a growth-rate question rather than as proof that the market expects the earnings to end. The margin test is in the bear case, and it is a real test. At the gross margin the company actually earned in the third quarter, sustained, with capex at its current share of revenue, the free cash flow after capex cannot service the debt, the DCF equity value falls to nothing, and the shares are worth only what the multiple legs pay on the last audited profit - Rp1,122 before the twelve-month carry. That is close to the market price of Rp1,115: the price is, to a first approximation, the value of a company that never recovers from the third-quarter margin [S0, S7]. We do not need the market to be wrong about durability, only wrong about permanence. The target of Rp2,463 is a fraction of the 3,260.9 of book value per share we forecast, so the call is a re-rating to a discount rather than a re-rating to a premium [S0].

The first risk is raw-material cost. Natural rubber, carbon black and synthetic rubber are priced in US dollars and moved by supply cycles the company cannot control, and the annual price adjustment lags them: the nine-month gross margin of 18.4% against the FY2025A 20.1% is the gap in action [S3, S7, S9]. If rubber stays high into 2027, the recovery to 20.1% that we assume by FY2029E is too early and the value is closer to the bear case.

The second risk is domestic demand. The 2026 rebound rests on a wholesale figure of 679,020 units in the nine months and an association target of 850,000 units that requires a strong fourth quarter [S8]. A stall in the vehicle market would hit the original-equipment channel first and the replacement channel with a lag, and because motorcycle tyres are the largest segment by volume and the closest to full utilisation, a slowdown there has an outsized effect on the group [S3].

The third risk is governance and the related-party channel, and it has two distinct halves. The first is transfer pricing and sourcing: related-party sales were 16.0% of net sales in FY2025A and rose to about a third in the nine months, the local channel now runs through PT Speedwork Solusi Utama, whose sales rose from a small base to 903 IDR bn in FY2025A while the company's investment in it is carried at nil, and the associates and the controlling group sit on the same side of the table [S3, S4]. If the channel shift is a transfer of margin rather than a distribution arrangement, the earnings base is worth less than the accounting profit implies, which is the argument for the discount rather than against it. The second half is credit, and it is concentrated rather than diversified: 2,101 IDR bn of the related-party receivable is owed by GITI Tire (USA) alone - a company under the controlling shareholder - against 1,251 IDR bn of sales to it in FY2025A, so the balance is trade credit of well over a year; GITI Tire Global Trading owes 494 IDR bn and GITI Tire (Canada) 7.3 IDR bn, and those three GITI trading companies account for the overwhelming majority of the 3,951 IDR bn book at 30 September 2026 [S3, S7]. A receivable that does not turn is either credit extended to the group's own distributor or a balance that will not be collected at the stated value; either way it is the largest single exposure in the balance sheet, and the allowance in the valuation bridge is sized on it rather than on a blended book [S7, S3].

The fourth risk is the capital programme. Management has said it plans a second plant at Karawang for electric-vehicle tyres, with an indicative cost of about ten trillion rupiah - roughly two and a half times the market capitalisation - but the source reports it as a plan rather than a board-approved commitment, so it is not in our base forecast [S5, S3]. We assign it to the bear case, where capex carries an explicit premium in every year of the forecast, and the funding requirement is met with debt rather than a rights issue; on that path free cash flow stays negative longer and the DCF value is destroyed rather than merely reduced [S5, S7]. The fifth risk is the supplier credit that is currently funding the working-capital build. Trade payables rose to 3,860 IDR bn from 2,049 IDR bn at the year-end against a cost of sales increase of about a tenth, so the balance sheet is borrowing from its suppliers at the same time as it lends to its controlling shareholder's trading companies; a supplier tightening terms would turn the net working-capital build into the gross one, and the company has no disclosed committed payables facility to replace it [S7]. The filing carries no cash-flow statement, so we cannot measure how much of the nine-month profit was cash-backed, and we treat that as the disclosure gap it is [S7]. The sixth risk is liquidity and index treatment: public shareholders hold 34.5% of the shares, above the regulatory floor, but turnover of IDR6.2bn a day is thin for an institution, and a change in index treatment or ownership rules would move the price more than the fundamentals [S0, S3].

The scenarios shock the same four drivers in both directions - revenue growth, gross margin, capex intensity and working capital - so the bear is not a stack of one-sided assumptions and the bull is not a free option. The gross-margin shocks are anchored on margins the company has actually earned, and each is applied to every forecast year rather than to the first alone: the bear shifts the whole path down by the distance from the base FY2026E margin to the third-quarter trough, so its first forecast year is the trough the quarter actually delivered and its terminal year stays far below any full-year margin the company has earned, while the bull shifts the whole path up by a deliberately smaller amount, so its first year is the last audited FY2025A margin and its terminal year ends fractionally above the FY2023A peak. The bull lift is compressed against a full mirror - which would carry the terminal year to a level no year in the file approaches - so the bull is not a free option, and it carries only the 20.0% probability [S3, S7]. The bear also carries the two balance-sheet consequences we can name - the Karawang plant proceeding into the downturn, and the supplier credit that funded the working-capital build being withdrawn - which is what turns a trough margin into a cash problem rather than an accounting one. At that margin the DCF equity value goes to nothing, so the bear's Rp1,122 comes from the multiple legs struck on the last audited profit, which is why the bear lands at the market price rather than far below it [S7, S0]. The probabilities are 30.0%, 50.0% and 20.0%; the bear is the higher tail because the governance and receivables evidence is live, not hypothetical [S4, S7]. The bull case values the shares at Rp4,468, a range wide enough that position sizing rather than the point estimate is the decision. The base case itself is the most likely path, not a cautious one: it assumes the FY2025A margin is recovered only by FY2029E and no more, and that capex falls to a steady-state percentage of revenue once the expansion is complete [S3, S7].

Signposts that would change our view are a quarterly gross margin above the FY2025A level, a fourth-quarter wholesale figure that misses the association's target, a rise in related-party receivables as a share of the total, a board decision to proceed with the electric-vehicle plant, and any change to the free float or index treatment [S8, S7, S5, S0].

Ownership is tightly held and the controlling chain runs through GITI. Denham Pte Ltd holds 49.5% and is majority-owned by GITI Tire Pte Ltd; Compagnie Financiere Michelin holds 10.0%; together they are a majority strategic block, while public shareholders outside the block hold 34.5% and Drs Lo Kheng Hong holds 5.9% [S3]. That ownership structure is the reason the shares trade below book, and it is not going to change: no share pledge is disclosed in the annual report we hold and there is no controlling-shareholder transaction in it [S3].

The same concentration is also the fastest route to closing the discount, and the report should say so. At roughly a third of book, a tender offer or take-private by Denham - or by Michelin, which has held ten per cent since the off-take agreement began and buys GT-made tyres for export - would be feasible at a large premium to the market and still be accretive to the buyer; the public float of 34.5% is large enough to be a real market and small enough that a controlling holder could absorb it [S3]. We do not put this in the base case, because there is no filed intention and no price signal, but it is the main bull-case route that is not an operating forecast, and it is why we resist a governance discount stacked on top of a market price that already embeds one [S3].

Related-party dealings are the main governance issue and they are large. Sales to related parties were 16.0% of net sales in FY2025A, with related-party trade receivables of 2,947 IDR bn at the year-end and 3,951 IDR bn at the end of September, and the nine-month channel data shows the local related-party line multiplying while the third-party local line fell [S3, S4, S7]. The counterparties are the controlling shareholder's own trading companies, not independent distributors: at 31 December 2025 GITI Tire (USA) accounted for 2,101 IDR bn of the related-party receivable, GITI Tire Global Trading 494 IDR bn and GITI Tire (Canada) 7.3 IDR bn, so roughly seven-eighths of the book sat with three companies under GITI Tire Pte Ltd - the majority owner of Denham [S3]. GITI Tire (USA)'s receivable is far larger than the trade that supports it: sales to it fell to 1,251 IDR bn in FY2025A from 1,765 IDR bn the year before while the receivable barely moved, which is a receivable of well over a year of purchases and the clearest sign that these balances are financing or that they are not trade at all [S3]. PT Speedwork Solusi Utama, the associate in which the company holds a small stake and which shares a key management member with the company, is the counterparty through which much of the domestic channel now runs, with sales of 903 IDR bn in FY2025A against a token amount a year earlier; the company's investment balance in it is nil, so the value of the relationship sits in the sales line rather than in an asset [S3]. The independent auditor, KAP Liana Ramon Xenia & Rekan, signed an unmodified opinion on the FY2025A accounts, and there is no qualification, emphasis of matter or restatement in the filing we hold [S3].

On the exchange regime, the shares have been listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 1990 and we treat them as investable: the FY2025A accounts carry an unmodified opinion, the 30 September 2026 statement is filed, and no notation letter, going-concern note or monitoring-board status appears in any document we hold [S3, S7]. We state the limitation plainly: the exchange's own site is outside the source registry this desk may cite, so board membership could not be confirmed positively in this revision, and the item is reported as checked-and-not-corroborated rather than as cleared. It matters because the special-monitoring board trades through a full call auction, which would break every entry and exit assumption behind the liquidity discount and the position size, and nothing we hold places GJTL on it [S10].

The dividend record is real but modest. The company paid Rp80.0 a share in FY2025A, up from the prior year's level, and there is no fixed payout policy beyond the company-law reserve requirement [S3, S0]. Our forecast holds the payout at 22.0%, the average of the last two years, which is a policy assumption rather than a commitment [S3].

On ESG, the material exposures are the rubber supply chain, energy use in curing, end-of-life tyres and labour. The company employs 17,626 people, runs its own polytechnic and reports community and training programmes, and the annual report we hold does not set a carbon-reduction target or a circular-economy commitment [S3, S5]. The export channel, including the Michelin-branded line, exposes the company to European and US sustainability requirements for tyres, which is a compliance cost rather than a current risk [S3].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the FY2026 results and annual report, the first-quarter 2027 volumes, the annual shareholders meeting and dividend decision, and the first-half 2027 financials. Between updates we monitor five series. The first is the monthly GAIKINDO wholesale figure, which is the cleanest high-frequency read on new-vehicle demand and therefore on the original-equipment channel [S8]. The second is the company's own quarterly revenue and gross margin, because the annual price adjustment shows up there first and the nine-month margin of 18.4% against the FY2025A 20.1% is the gap the thesis has to close [S7, S3].

The third is working capital: inventories of 3,461 IDR bn and related-party receivables of 3,951 IDR bn against third-party receivables of 1,578 IDR bn at the end of September are the line items that determine whether free cash flow turns positive on the schedule we assume [S7]. The fourth is the capital programme, where any board approval of the electric-vehicle plant or a further expansion of truck and bus radial capacity would change the capex path and therefore the DCF [S5, S3]. The fifth is ownership and index treatment, where the public float of 34.5% and the controlling block of Denham and Michelin are the variables that govern the discount [S3].

The single number that decides the year is the gross margin. If the FY2026 annual report shows the margin back at or above the FY2025A level of 20.1%, the recovery we assume from FY2027E is ahead of schedule and the target has room; if it is still at the nine-month level of 18.4%, the base case is intact but the market's scepticism is justified and the bear case becomes the reference [S3, S7]. We would revisit the rating on a sustained margin recovery, a reduction in related-party receivables, or a decision on the new plant that preserves free cash flow.

bear.narrative: Domestic car demand stalls after the 2026 rebound and raw-material costs stay high, so the gross margin falls to the 13.9% the third quarter actually earned and only edges up from there instead of recovering to the last audited level; the GITI trading companies cannot absorb further volume, the related-party receivable is written down and suppliers pull back the credit that funded the working-capital build; the Karawang plant proceeds into the downturn, so capex stays above base and the cash pile drains.

bull.narrative: The domestic replacement cycle runs a second year as GAIKINDO volumes approach the 850,000 target and the Speedwork channel keeps scaling, rubber costs ease and the annual price adjustment restores the gross margin to the last audited FY2025A level a year ahead of the base case and carries it above that level through the forecast, ending fractionally above the FY2023A peak; the TBR expansion lands on time, the Karawang plant stays on the drawing board, and the working-capital build reverses as the GITI balances are collected.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +8.0% is built from the nine months, not assumed: 9M2026 net sales were Rp14,322.5bn against Rp13,122.0bn, +9.1%, but the mix moved violently - local related-party sales rose from Rp320.46bn to Rp3.14tn while local third-party sales fell from Rp10.21tn to Rp8.62tn, and export third-party sales fell from Rp1.5tn to Rp1.04tn [S4, S7]. Carrying the fourth quarter at +4.7% on the Rp4,542.2bn of Q4 2025 (below the third quarter's +15.7% because the prior-year fourth quarter already contained a strong domestic push) gives FY2026E revenue of about Rp19,077bn [S7, S0]. FY2027E-FY2030E +4.0% assumes the related-party channel stabilises and total growth reverts to the underlying replacement market - the Indonesian PCR and truck tyre market grew 2.0% in 2025, with replacement +3.6% - plus the TBR capacity added in 2025 (3,200 units a day from 2,900), rather than extrapolating the 9M related-party surge [S3, S8, S4]. The long run is the house 4.0% terminal growth, so no growth is capitalised forever [S3, S8].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 18.1% is built from the actual quarters, not from a full-year plug: the nine months earned Rp2,640.5bn on Rp14,322.5bn, 18.4% [S7, S6], and the stand-alone third quarter earned 13.9% (Rp738.5bn on Rp5,323.2bn) - the lowest three-month margin in the pack's series and down from 19.5% in the second quarter and 23.0% in the first, as raw-material costs rose from the second quarter and the annual price adjustment lagged [S0, S6]. We carry the fourth quarter at 17.1% of the implied Rp4,754.8bn of revenue: above the third-quarter trough, because the annual price adjustment lands partly in the quarter and the pack's own 2025 path recovered 5.6pp from the second quarter to the fourth, but 6.2pp below the 23.3% the prior-year fourth quarter earned, because input costs are higher this year [S0, S9]. The previous 20.5% fourth quarter required a 6.4pp one-quarter rebound that no quarter in the file has produced in either direction, and it also sat above the FY2027E average - internally inconsistent with the delayed recovery we describe [S7, S0]. The history is FY2023A 22.0%, FY2024A 21.5%, FY2025A 20.1% and 9M2026 18.4% [S3, S7]. S9 (July 2026) reports raw-material prices rising at a double-digit rate and the company absorbing them to protect distributors, so the recovery is delayed a year: FY2027E 19.2% and FY2028E 19.7% now sit above the fourth-quarter 2026 exit rate, as a recovery that is starting must, and from FY2029E, including the long run, the margin is FY2025A's 20.1%, the last audited full-year margin, so no part of the terminal value depends on a margin above history [S3, S9].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Selling plus general and administrative expenses were Rp1,348.3bn in the nine months of 2026 (Rp761.1bn selling plus Rp587.2bn administration) on revenue of Rp14,322.5bn, 9.41%, against 9.94% in the nine months of 2025, so operating leverage is positive as revenue grows [S7]. The engine's history uses the data pack's net opex (FY2025A Rp1,706.5bn, 9.66% of revenue), which nets other operating income [S0]. FY2026E 9.46% carries the fourth quarter at 9.6% of the quarter's revenue, the year-end accrual pattern, and the ratio is then held at 9.55% to FY2030E and in the long run: no cost programme is disclosed, and holding it is the neutral assumption [S7, S3].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack carries Rp105.5bn of depreciation for FY2025; the audited note shows Rp802.8bn (Rp697.3bn in manufacturing cost, Rp15.4bn in selling, Rp90.0bn in administration), 4.54% of revenue, with Rp752.2bn in FY2024 [S3]. That is restated as facts and the engine rebuilds EBITDA from it. FY2026E is held at 4.52% of revenue (about Rp878bn) because capex of Rp2,271bn in FY2025 was well above the charge and the TBR line is still ramping, easing to 4.40% by FY2030E as additions normalise against a larger asset base [S3, S7].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capital expenditure was Rp2,271bn in FY2025 (12.9% of revenue) against Rp1,421bn in FY2024, directed at the TBR capacity expansion and at maintenance, and funded from operating cash flow, an investment credit facility and a syndicated loan [S3]. The nine months of 2026 lifted net fixed assets from Rp10,563.3bn to Rp11,823.0bn, so FY2026E is set at 12.6% of revenue (about Rp2,448bn) with advances for plant and equipment still at Rp1,145.8bn at 30 September [S7]. FY2027E 10.5% and FY2028E 9.0% assume the TBR project completes and spend falls back; from FY2029E 8.0% and a 7.0% long run, which is depreciation of about 4.4% plus the asset base needed for 4% growth, i.e. steady state rather than a haircut. The decline from 12.6% to 7.0% is a sourced view that the expansion is discrete, not a cautious one [S3, S7].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A operating working capital was Rp3,382.7bn, 19.15% of revenue, on the pack's definition (current assets less current liabilities plus current debt less cash) [S0]. At 30 September 2026 the same definition gives Rp3,899.4bn on current assets of Rp10,612.9bn, current liabilities of Rp7,852.6bn, current debt of Rp1,966.9bn and cash of Rp827.8bn, about 20.1% of our FY2026E revenue [S7]. Both documented channels are building: inventories are Rp3,460.6bn against Rp2,576.1bn at the prior year-end (+34% against cost of sales +9.9%) and related-party receivables are Rp3,950.6bn against Rp2,946.9bn, while trade payables also rose to Rp3,859.8bn, which is why the net ratio moves less than the gross lines [S7]. We hold 20.1% easing to 19.8%, and put a further build in the bear case [S7].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The nine months of 2026 carried an effective 21.7% (tax Rp268.0bn on pre-tax profit Rp1,232.9bn) against 23.6% in FY2025A and 23.9% in FY2024A; 22.0%, the statutory rate, holds the forecast [S7, S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs were Rp453.8bn in FY2025 on opening debt of Rp5,092.9bn, 8.9%, and Rp300.0bn in the nine months of 2026, an annualised Rp400.0bn on opening debt of Rp5,205.7bn, 7.7% [S3, S7]. The rate is falling as the US-dollar notes were refinanced into rupiah bank facilities in January 2025 and the rupiah policy rate is 5.75% in the house macro deck; 7.7% holds the last period [S3, S7].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was Rp20.8bn in FY2025 on opening cash of Rp1,401.4bn and Rp12.5bn in the nine months of 2026 on opening cash of Rp925.2bn, 1.35-1.48%; 1.5% holds it [S3, S7, S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt rose from Rp5,205.7bn at the end of 2025 to Rp5,860.6bn at 30 September 2026 (short-term bank loans Rp1,245.9bn, current maturities Rp721.0bn, long-term Rp3,893.6bn) as negative free cash flow after a Rp2,271bn capex year and the Rp278.8bn dividend was funded with debt [S7, S3]. FY2026E +900 holds our capex and dividend assumption; FY2027E +400 and FY2028E +100 fund the tail of the expansion; FY2029E-FY2030E turn to repayment of 300-500 a year as capex falls below operating cash flow [S7, S3].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The engine derives this line from the filing as profit before tax less EBIT plus interest; FY2025A was +Rp175.6bn, including a Rp96.0bn foreign-exchange gain and the associates' loss, and FY2024A was -Rp43.4bn on a Rp34.8bn exchange loss [S3, S0]. The nine months of 2026 already contain a Rp150.0bn exchange gain, Rp50.7bn of other gains and Rp27.5bn of associate income, so FY2026E carries about Rp250bn of realised non-operating income plus a small fourth quarter [S7]. From FY2027E the line is normalised to +Rp60bn, which is associate income around the recent run-rate plus a modest other gain and no forecast exchange gain: the rupiah is a scenario risk, not an earnings stream [S7, S3].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: There is no minority interest in the consolidated accounts: profit is attributable wholly to the owners of the parent in FY2024A, FY2025A and 9M2026 [S3, S7].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend was Rp80 a share, Rp278.8bn in total, 22.4% of FY2025 net profit of Rp1,243.2bn, up from Rp50 a share on FY2024 [S0, S3]. The company has no fixed payout policy beyond the company-law reserve requirement, so 22.0% holds the last two years rather than an engine default struck on a year in which the prior year's dividend was the cash item [S3, S0].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Share count is unchanged at 3,484.4586m (3,484.8m issued less 341,400 treasury shares) and no corporate action is disclosed [S3, S7].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House IDR terminal growth is 4.0%, but the model's terminal ROE is about nine per cent against a WACC of 12.0% (inside the house 11-13% band), so growth above 3.5% would not be value-accretive on the company's own returns and the terminal ROIC fade the method card requires is in the rate, not in an above-history margin; 3.5% is also below the nominal GDP growth implied by the macro deck and below our FY2026E exit rate [S3, S7]. The terminal-g case is argued on the WACC, the rate that discounts the forecast, not on the cost of equity used for the twelve-month carry.

challenges.challenge: The base case carries Q4 2026 at a 20.3% gross margin (the 18.9% full-year input less the 2,640.5 nine-month gross profit on 4,754.8 of implied Q4 revenue). The stand-alone Q3 2026 margin is 13.9% (gross profit 738.457 on revenue 5,323.245), and the pack's three 2026 quarters sum to the filing's 2,640.509 exactly, so this is not a vendor artefact. The report never states the Q3 figure and describes the Q4 requirement only as 'above the nine-month average' (18.4%), which implies a 1.9pp step; the actual step is 6.4pp in one quarter, in a quarter S9 says input costs were still rising. The basis text says 20.5%, which does not reconcile with the 18.9% input either.
challenges.answer: Arithmetic accepted. FY2026E gross margin cut to 18.1% and the fourth quarter now carried at 17.1% on the implied Rp4,754.8bn, not 20.3%. The assumption basis states the Q3 stand-alone 13.9% (Rp738.5bn on Rp5,323.2bn) and sources the 6.4pp step against the pack's 2025 Q2-to-Q4 recovery of 5.6pp; section 3 now says the quarter was the lowest margin in the file, and the basis, the model input and the report agree [S7, S0, S6].

challenges.challenge: The bear's gross margin is base minus 1.5pp, i.e. 17.4% for FY2026E, which is 3.5pp above the 13.9% the company earned in Q3 2026 and only 1.0pp below the nine-month 18.4%. On the driver section 7 calls the single number that decides the year, the downside case is a better-than-current-quarter case. Round one asked for a scenario anchored on the 9M run-rate (C7) and the revision still has none; the bear narrative's receivable impairment still has no corresponding shock.
challenges.answer: Bear reset to the Q3 actual: the -4.2pp gross-margin shock takes FY2026E to 13.9%, with revenue -3.0pp, capex +1.5pp and nwc +3.0pp so supplier credit normalising and the Karawang build are shocks, and the GITI receivable allowance is carried in every scenario. Bear v0 Rp1,121 and bear target Rp1,300, at or below the Rp1,115 spot; section 5 discloses that the DCF is floored there and the bear value comes from the multiple legs [S7, S0, S3].

challenges.challenge: The working-capital build is being funded by suppliers, and the report treats that only as an arithmetic offset. Trade payables rose from 2,049.2 to 3,859.8 (+88.4%) while cost of sales rose about 10%, against inventories 2,576.1 to 3,460.6 (+34.3%) and related-party receivables 2,946.9 to 3,950.6 (+34.1%). Rp1,810.6bn of new supplier credit is what makes cash conversion look tolerable; no risk item or scenario covers suppliers tightening, and S7 has no cash flow statement, so nine-month operating cash flow is unknown.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now quantifies the supplier dependence: trade payables 2,049.2 to 3,859.8 (+88.4%) against cost of sales up about a tenth, Rp1,810.6bn of new supplier credit offsetting the 884.5 inventory and 1,003.7 related-party receivable build. It states plainly that S7 has no cash-flow statement, so nine-month operating cash flow cannot be computed; payables normalising is named as risk 5 and modelled as the bear's nwc shock [S7].

challenges.challenge: The extreme-call justification and section 3 say the nine-month working-capital build has 'absorbed more than the period's profit'. On the report's own NWC definition the build is 516.7bn (3,899.4 at 30 September against 3,382.7 at FY2025A), well below the 964.9bn profit; the 1.89tn gross build in inventories plus related-party receivables is offset by 1.81tn of extra payables. The sentence carries the 'earnings are no longer cash-backed' conclusion and overstates the drag.
challenges.answer: Claim withdrawn. Section 3 and section 4 now carry the net figure and the gross-to-net bridge: inventories +884.5 and related-party receivables +1,003.7 against payables +1,810.6, a net NWC build of 516.7 against nine-month profit of 964.9, and say the build is borrowed from suppliers rather than that earnings are unbacked [S7, S0].

challenges.challenge: The reverse-DCF paragraph ('cannot bracket the market price at all ... the market is not pricing slow growth but non-durable earnings') rests on model.reverse_dcf, which is available=false with target a.revenue_growth: the engine flexes revenue growth only and holds the 20.1% terminal margin and both multiple legs fixed. The DCF equity value is 6,025bn against a market 3,885bn, and a 35% gap on a 20.1% terminal margin is a margin question, not a growth-rate question. The report never runs the reverse DCF on margin, so the rhetorical conclusion is not supported by the test performed.
challenges.answer: Withdrawn. Section 4 now says the engine's reverse DCF flexes revenue growth only, that it cannot bracket the market price, and reads that as evidence the gap is a margin question rather than proof of non-durable earnings. The margin test is stated explicitly: at the 13.9% the third quarter earned the DCF equity value falls to nothing and the shares are worth only the multiple legs' Rp1,121, close to spot [S0, S7].
